subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: risk assessment and safety planning [Action]
passage: When our school's eco club announced a rally to save the old park trees, I wanted to go, but Mummy's face said no before her mouth did. So I made a checklist. First I read the notice again: the district office had given permission and the organisers called it a peaceful gathering. Then I told my parents the exact spot, the gate near the library, and that it would run from four to six. My uncle Zubin agreed to come along. I packed two bottles of water and charged my phone to full, and Uncle and I decided that if the crowd got tight or the mood changed, we would leave by the library lane at half past five at the latest. Mummy still looked worried, but she stopped saying no. Standing there with my sign, I felt calm, because the exit was already decided. — Imran

qa.q: Where did Imran tell the family the rally would be?
qa.a: At the gate near the library, from four to six.

qa.q: How did Imran feel at the rally, and what explains it?
qa.a: Calm, because the exit was already decided and the plan had been checked with the family.

qa.q: What could Imran do if the parents still refused, and why?
qa.a: Imran could back the cause another way, such as signing a petition or helping with a school poster, because it keeps the aim without adding risk the family is not comfortable with.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the plan?
qa.a: Mummy still looked worried, but a known place, set timings, an adult companion and a fixed leaving time gave her something concrete to trust.

grounding: A teen checks the protest is permitted and peaceful, tells parents the place, goes with an adult, packs supplies and agrees a leaving time.

passage:
Note from Siddharth's aunt, who went along

Siddharth asked to join the students' silent march for a new school crossing on the Pune-Satara road. His parents were away, so I spoke with him first.

He had already checked: the march had police permission, the route was published, and the organisers were the parents' association. He had also read their rules: no blocking traffic, no slogans against anyone. I said I would come.

Before we left, he told his parents the location by phone. He packed water, a charged phone and a snack. We agreed with his friend Sarika and her father that the four of us would stay together, and that if any shouting began, we would leave by the side lane near the temple.

The march was calm and took forty minutes. We left at 6:15 as planned. On the way back, Siddharth asked how the association would follow up. I have asked them to send him the update.

qa.q: Who were the organisers of the march?
How might Siddharth have felt preparing so carefully for the march?
qa.a: He probably felt responsible and a little nervous, wanting to take part while making sure it was safe.

qa.q: What else could Siddharth do to stay involved after the march?
qa.a: He could follow up with the parents' association or write to the local council, keeping his involvement going through lawful steps.

qa.q: How does the plan look to Sarika's father?
qa.a: Sarika's father likely felt reassured, since an adult was going, the route and exit were agreed, and everyone knew to stay together.

grounding: A caregiver's note shows a teen checking a protest is lawful and peaceful, telling parents, going with a trusted adult, carrying water and a charged phone, and agreeing when to leave.

passage:
Thursday night

The climate march is on Saturday and I really want to go. But I didn't want to just turn up like last time, when that street thing got scary and I had no plan.

So today I did the boring stuff. I checked the city police website: the march has permission, the route is from the park to the town hall. The organisers are a students' environment group that my science teacher knows. Their notice says peaceful, no masks, no damage.

At dinner I told Amma and Appa the route and the timings. Appa said he'd come if I wanted. Alka's aunt is going too, so we'll be a group of five.

I've packed water, charged the power bank, and saved Amma's number as the first speed dial. We agreed: if it turns angry or the crowd gets too tight, we walk out by the library road, no arguing.

I'm Harsha, and for once I feel excited instead of nervous.

qa.q: What route will the march take?
qa.a: From the park to the town hall.

qa.q: How does Harsha feel about going to this march?
qa.a: Harsha feels excited rather than nervous, thanks to the careful planning.

qa.q: What else could Harsha add to the plan?
qa.a: Harsha could agree on a meeting point in case the group gets separated, since phones can fail in crowds.

qa.q: How might Amma and Appa see Harsha's preparation?
qa.a: They probably feel reassured and trusted, since Harsha shared the route and timings and Appa could choose to come along.

grounding: A diary shows a teen checking a march is lawful and peaceful, telling parents, going with trusted adults, packing water and a charged phone and agreeing when to leave.
